title: Git and GitHub
eyebrow: Delivery workflow · Remember, compare, share, review, and recover
summary: Learn Git by following a project through real state changes: edit files, choose what belongs in the next saved snapshot, commit it, branch safely, share it with another repository, review it on GitHub, automate checks, and recover from mistakes.
prerequisites: None. Knowing how to open a terminal helps with the command examples, but every Git state used here is explained before the command that changes it.
learningOutcomes: Explain where an edit exists before staging, after staging, after committing, and after pushing.
Explain commits, branches, HEAD, remotes, merge, rebase, fetch, pull requests, and Actions from the state changes they represent.
Choose a safer recovery move by first identifying whether the work is uncommitted, committed only locally, or already published.

heroVisual.title: A change moves through several different places
heroVisual.caption: The same file edit can exist only in your working files, be selected for the next commit, become durable Git history, be published to another repository, and then be reviewed or deployed.

nodes.label: Working files
nodes.detail: What is currently on disk in the checked-out project.

nodes.label: Staging area
nodes.detail: The exact content you have selected for the next commit.

nodes.label: Commit
nodes.detail: A saved project snapshot connected to earlier history.

nodes.label: Remote repository
nodes.detail: Another Git repository, commonly hosted on GitHub.

nodes.label: Pull request and checks
nodes.detail: GitHub compares proposed history and coordinates review and automation.

nodes.label: Authoritative branch
nodes.detail: The accepted history can become the release or deployment source.

sections.title: 1. Git solves the problem of remembering project states
sections.summary: Saving files tells you what exists now. Version control also needs to answer what changed, who recorded it, which earlier state it came from, and how to return to known history safely.

blocks.text: Imagine a small site that works on Monday, gains search on Tuesday, and breaks while you are changing navigation on Wednesday. Three folders named final, final-2, and final-really-final cannot reliably explain which changes belong together or how Wednesday relates to Tuesday. Git is a distributed version-control system: it records project history as identifiable commits so you can compare states, create parallel lines of work, exchange history with other repositories, and recover with evidence instead of guesswork.

items.title: Repository
items.summary: The Git history and references for a project, plus usually a working tree where you edit checked-out files.

items.title: Commit
items.summary: A recorded project snapshot with metadata and a link to one or more parent commits.

items.title: Diff
items.summary: A comparison that shows how content differs between two states, such as your working file and the committed version.

blocks.prompt: If you edit a file and press Save in your editor, has Git automatically created a commit?
blocks.explanation: Saving changes the working file on disk. A Git commit is a separate intentional history operation. This distinction is the foundation for understanding status, staging, committing, and recovery.

sections.title: 2. An edit moves from working files to the next snapshot to committed history
sections.summary: The staging area exists so you can decide exactly which current changes belong together in the next commit.

visual.title: One local change, three states
visual.caption: Inspect first. Stage only what belongs together. Review that staged snapshot before recording it.

nodes.label: Working tree
nodes.detail: Files as they currently exist on disk after your edits.

nodes.label: Index · staging area
nodes.detail: Git's proposed content for the next commit.

nodes.label: Commit
nodes.detail: The selected snapshot is recorded in repository history.

blocks.text: Git calls the checked-out project files the working tree. The staging area, also called the index, holds the exact content proposed for the next commit. This extra step matters because your working tree can contain several experiments while one commit should usually record one coherent change.

blocks.code:
git status
git diff
git add src/search.ts tests/search.test.ts
git diff --staged
git commit -m "feat: add typo-tolerant topic search"
blocks.explanation: status summarizes the known states. git diff shows unstaged working-tree changes. git add copies the selected versions of two paths into the index. git diff --staged reviews what the next commit will contain. git commit records that staged snapshot and advances the current branch to the new commit.

blocks.title: Staging is selection, not backup
blocks.body: A staged edit is not a durable replacement for a commit and should not be treated as a backup. Commit coherent work when it is ready to become history, and use an appropriate backup strategy for data that Git is not meant to protect.

blocks.prompt: You edit app.ts and README.md, but stage only app.ts. What will the next commit contain if you commit now?
blocks.answer: The staged version of app.ts, not the unstaged README.md edit.
blocks.explanation: A normal commit records the index, not every current working-tree difference. That is why reviewing git diff --staged is a precise pre-commit check.

sections.title: 3. Commits connect into history; branches are names that point into that history
sections.summary: Once saved snapshots make sense, the commit graph, branch references, HEAD, and tags become much less mysterious.

visual.title: History is connected commits plus names
visual.caption: A, B, C, and D are commits. Names such as main and feature/search point to commits and can move as new commits are created.

nodes.label: A ← B
nodes.detail: B records A as its parent, connecting the newer snapshot to earlier history.

nodes.label: main → B
nodes.detail: main is a branch reference currently pointing at commit B.

nodes.label: feature/search → C
nodes.detail: A separate branch can advance to C while main still points at B.

nodes.label: tag v1.0 → B
nodes.detail: A tag can give a stable human-readable name to a particular commit.

blocks.text: Each normal commit stores a parent identifier pointing to the commit it follows. Those parent links create a directed history graph: newer commits point back toward their parent history. A branch is not a folder or a second copy of the whole project; it is a movable reference, usually pointing to the newest commit in one line of work.

items.title: Parent
items.summary: The earlier commit a new commit directly follows. A merge commit can have more than one parent.

items.title: Branch
items.summary: A movable reference to a commit. Creating a new commit while a branch is checked out normally advances that branch reference.

items.title: HEAD
items.summary: Git's reference for what is currently checked out. In the common case, HEAD refers to the current branch, which then points to a commit.

items.title: Tag
items.summary: A named reference commonly used to mark a particular release or milestone rather than advancing with each new commit.

blocks.prompt: If main points to commit D, is main itself a container holding the files from D?
blocks.explanation: main is a reference that names a commit. The commit identifies a saved snapshot and its history. Thinking 'branch = movable name' prevents many misunderstandings about switching, merging, and deleting branches.

sections.title: 4. Branches let work diverge; merge and rebase change how histories come together
sections.summary: Integration is about constructing the intended final history and code, not merely making conflict markers disappear.

rows: Merge
Combines histories, either by fast-forwarding a reference or by creating a commit with multiple parent histories.
A true merge commit preserves the fact that lines of history diverged and were joined.
Rebase
Replays selected commits onto a new base so they receive new parents.
Replayed commits get new identities; avoid casually rewriting history other people already depend on.
Cherry-pick
Applies the change represented by selected commits onto the current history.
It creates new commit identities and can duplicate a logical change if used without understanding existing history.
Revert
Creates a new commit whose change reverses the effect of an earlier commit.
Published history remains intact, which is often safer for shared authoritative branches.
blocks.caption: Choose the operation from the history outcome you actually need

blocks.text: A conflict means Git cannot automatically combine competing changes with enough confidence. It is not proof that Git failed. Read both intended behaviors, edit the result you actually want, run tests and other checks, and review the complete diff. Resolving markers without understanding behavior can create a clean-looking but incorrect merge.

items: Know the target history before running an integration command.
Update your knowledge of the target branch before final review.
Resolve intended behavior, not only text conflicts.
Run focused tests and regression checks after the histories are combined.
Do not force-push shared authoritative history unless rewriting it is an explicit, coordinated decision.

sections.title: 5. A remote is another Git repository, not a magical cloud copy of your folder
sections.summary: Fetch learns what another repository has. Push asks that repository to move one of its references. Pull combines fetching with a local integration step.

visual.title: Local names and remote knowledge are separate
visual.caption: Keeping the references distinct makes fetch, push, and pull easier to reason about.

nodes.label: main
nodes.detail: Your local branch reference.

nodes.label: origin
nodes.detail: A conventional local name for another repository connection. The name is not inherently special.

nodes.label: origin/main
nodes.detail: A local remote-tracking reference representing the remote main state known from the last fetch.

nodes.label: Remote main
nodes.detail: The actual branch reference in the remote repository.

blocks.code:
git fetch origin
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git push origin feature/search
blocks.explanation: fetch downloads objects and updates remote-tracking knowledge such as origin/main without merging those commits into your current local branch. The log command lets you inspect the resulting history. push asks origin to publish the local feature/search history by updating the corresponding remote reference when GitHub's permissions and history rules allow it.

blocks.title: Upstream branch
blocks.body: A local branch can be configured to track an upstream branch. That relationship gives commands such as status, pull, and push a default branch to compare or exchange with; it does not make the two references the same object.

blocks.title: git pull is more than 'download'
blocks.body: pull first fetches and then integrates according to configuration or command options, commonly by merge or rebase. If you need to inspect remote history before changing your current branch, fetch first and integrate explicitly.

blocks.prompt: You run git fetch origin and receive new commits for origin/main. Must your local main now contain those commits?
blocks.explanation: Fetch updates local knowledge of the remote repository. Your local main moves only when you intentionally integrate or otherwise update it. This separation is useful because it lets you inspect incoming history before changing your current branch.

sections.title: 6. GitHub adds review, permissions, policy, and collaboration around Git history
sections.summary: Git supplies commits and references. GitHub can host the repository and coordinate proposals, discussion, checks, approvals, releases, issues, and access rules around that history.

items.title: Publish the proposed branch
items.explanation: Push the commits so GitHub can see the exact head of the proposed work.
items.result: Humans and automation can inspect the same commit history.

items.title: Open a pull request
items.explanation: A pull request is a GitHub collaboration object comparing proposed changes with a target branch. State why the change exists, what changed, how it was checked, and what risk remains.
items.result: The integration proposal has one review surface.

items.title: Attach automated evidence
items.explanation: CI can build, test, lint, validate schemas, run security checks, or enforce repository policy against the proposed commit.
items.result: Repeatable evidence is attached to the exact revision under review.

items.title: Review behavior and diff
items.explanation: Humans examine correctness, maintainability, UX, security, omissions, and whether the change belongs in the target branch.

items.title: Integrate using repository policy
items.explanation: Merge, squash, or rebase according to the history contract for that repository.
items.result: The authoritative target reference advances to accepted history.

blocks.title: A pull request is not a core Git object
blocks.body: Git itself knows commits, trees, references, remotes, and related repository data. A pull request is GitHub's hosted workflow for comparing branches and coordinating review, checks, approvals, and integration.

items: Use a title that describes the outcome, not merely the files changed.
Explain why the work exists, what changed, how it was verified, and remaining risk.
Review the actual diff for secrets, unrelated refactors, generated noise, and missing tests.
Require evidence against the exact commit that will be integrated when repository policy depends on checks.

sections.title: 7. GitHub Actions turns repository events into repeatable jobs
sections.summary: A workflow is automation defined in repository YAML. An event starts it, jobs run on declared environments, steps execute actions or commands, and permissions limit what the workflow token can do.

visual.title: From repository event to evidence or delivery
visual.caption: Understanding this chain makes CI/CD configuration easier to debug and secure.

nodes.label: Event
nodes.detail: Something such as a pull request, push, schedule, or manual dispatch triggers a workflow.

nodes.label: Workflow
nodes.detail: The YAML file selects which jobs should run for that event.

nodes.label: Job
nodes.detail: A job receives a runner and permissions and contains ordered steps.

nodes.label: Steps
nodes.detail: Actions and shell commands check out code, install tools, test, build, package, or deploy.

nodes.label: Evidence or artifact
nodes.detail: The run produces pass/fail evidence, logs, packages, or deployable output.

blocks.code:
name: Verify

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm check
blocks.explanation: pull_request limits the event to proposed changes targeting main. contents: read gives the workflow token read-only repository-content access at the workflow level. The job runs on a GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runner. The external actions are pinned to immutable commit SHAs, the dependency graph comes from the lockfile, and pnpm check runs the project's own verification contract.

items.title: Continuous integration · CI
items.summary: Run repeatable checks when changes are proposed or integrated.

items.title: Continuous delivery
items.summary: Produce a verified deployable result while a separate decision may control whether it is released.
items.example: build and upload a release artifact

items.title: Continuous deployment
items.summary: Automatically publish verified changes that meet the repository's deployment policy.

blocks.title: Workflow code has real authority
blocks.body: Treat Actions as privileged automation. Minimize token permissions, protect secrets, review untrusted pull-request inputs, and pin third-party actions according to repository supply-chain policy. A full commit SHA is the immutable way to pin an action revision.

sections.title: 8. Recover by identifying where the unwanted change exists
sections.summary: The safest first move depends on whether the change is only in working files, staged, committed locally, or already shared with other people and systems.

rows: Working file changed incorrectly
Inspect git diff, then restore only the intended path if you are certain the edit is disposable.
Do not destroy unrelated uncommitted work.
Wrong change staged
Remove it from the index while keeping the working-tree edit if the edit is still useful.
Staged and working content are separate states.
Local unpublished commit needs correction
Amend or rewrite local history only after confirming nobody else depends on that commit identity.
Unpublished history has a smaller coordination boundary.
Published change must be undone
Prefer a new revert commit when preserving shared history is the repository contract.
The corrective change is explicit without rewriting others' known history.
Secret was committed
Revoke or rotate the secret immediately, then follow the provider/repository history-removal procedure.
Removing one visible commit does not make an exposed credential trustworthy again.
Branch reference was deleted
Find the still-existing commit using another reference, known identifier, or reflog before unreachable objects are eventually pruned.
Deleting a branch name does not necessarily delete the commit object immediately.
blocks.caption: Recovery starts with the publication boundary and the exact state you want to preserve

blocks.title: Do not run destructive Git commands from memory
blocks.body: Before reset, clean, restore, force push, or history rewriting, inspect status, relevant diffs, the commit graph, remotes, and the exact command documentation. Make the desired final state explicit first.

items: State what must be preserved before changing repository state.
Create a temporary safety branch or tag when recovery risk is high and a reference will help.
Understand whether the commit is already published or referenced elsewhere.
Verify both the original software behavior and git status/history after recovery.

glossary.definition: Git's stored project history and references, commonly used with a checked-out working tree.
The checked-out project files on disk that you directly edit.
Git's proposed content for the next commit.
A recorded project snapshot with metadata and one or more parent links connecting it to history.
A movable Git reference that usually points at the newest commit in one line of work.
Git's reference identifying what is currently checked out; commonly it points to the current branch.
A named configuration for communicating with another Git repository.
A local reference such as origin/main that records the remote branch state known from the last fetch.
A GitHub collaboration object for reviewing and integrating proposed changes between branches.
GitHub Actions automation defined in YAML and triggered by configured repository events.
A local log of recent updates to references and HEAD that can help locate previously known commits during recovery.
